This guidance is intended to support local authorities and fire and rescue services in carrying out their statutory functions in relation to buildings covered by the developer remediation contract (the Contract). It provides an overview of the purpose and scope of the Contract, which incorporates the self-remediation terms. It explains the obligations placed on signatory developers (referred to as Participant Developers) and is intended to promote a consistent and coordinated approach between regulators, Participant Developers and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG).

It also supports a shared understanding of how the Contract interacts with existing regulatory regimes and how information should be shared effectively. MHCLG will keep this guidance under review and may revise it periodically to reflect user feedback and changes relevant policy or legal frameworks.

This guidance provides general guidance only. It does not constitute legal advice. Regulators should seek their own legal advice where appropriate. The developer remediation contract creates a legal relationship between the Secretary of State and each Participant Developer. This guidance refers to relevant provisions of the publicly available self-remediation terms, which are annexed to each Contract, but does not otherwise comment on that legal relationship.

For ease of reference, where this guidance refers to clauses, obligations or requirements under the Contract, these should be read as references to the self-remediation terms contained in Schedule 1 to the Contract. Capitalised terms are as defined in Annex 1 of the self-remediation terms. The developer remediation contract, the self-remediation terms, relevant Annexes, and a published list of Participant Developers are available on GOV.UK: Developer remediation contract.

Developer remediation contract

Overview of the developer remediation contract

The Contract, which incorporates the self-remediation terms (SRTs), is a contract which 53 major developers have signed with the Secretary of State. Each contract creates binding legal obligations on both the developers and the Secretary of State. By entering into the Contract, the developers have made binding commitments to address historic life-critical fire safety defects in residential buildings they developed or refurbished in England over a 30-year period. Developers that have signed the Contract are referred to as ‘Participant Developers’. Further information on the Contract is available on GOV.UK: Developer remediation contract.

The Contract is underpinned by the Responsible Actors Scheme. The Scheme was established by regulations made under sections 126-129 of the Building Safety Act 2022, which provides the statutory framework supporting developer obligations in this area. Regulations enable Ministers to impose prohibitions on developers in certain circumstances.

Find out if a building is covered by the Contract or whether a developer has signed the Contract

MHCLG sends data to local regulators every quarter which includes a list of buildings covered by the Contract. You can check whether a building in your jurisdiction is covered by the Contract by referring to this data. Further information on this data share is elaborated in the “Data about buildings covered by the Contract” section of this guidance.

If you want to know whether a developer has signed the Contract, you can check the list of signatories: Developer remediation contract.

Buildings in scope of the Contract

The Contract applies to residential buildings that are 11 metres or more in height, located in England, which a Participant Developer (or one of its group companies) developed or refurbished during the 30‑year period ending on 4 April 2022. Under the Contract, height is measured in accordance with Building Regulation 2010, Approved Document B, Diagram D6. Ownership, management arrangements or freehold interests are not relevant to a developer’s liability in respect of a building.

The Contract requires Participant Developers to identify all buildings that fall within the scope of the Contract (regardless of whether they require works). If works are required, then Participant Developers are required to carry out the necessary works and demonstrate that those works have been completed in line with the relevant standards.

As of July 2026, the 53 developers who signed the Contract have identified over 4,500 buildings (see definition of “Building” in Annex 1 of the SRTs) covered by the Contract, of which over 2,500 have been found to require remedial works. These figures exclude buildings being remediated through government-funded schemes, where developers are responsible for reimbursing government. The latest published data on this is available on GOV.UK: Building regulation.

If anyone has concerns about the external wall system of a building and believes that it should be covered by the Contract and is not, they can flag it at Tell Homes England about unsafe cladding on a building.

Defects covered by the Contract

‘Defect’ is defined in Annex 1 of the Contract to cover defects, faults, shrinkage or other failings that give rise to a life-critical fire safety risk in a building, and which arose from the design, construction or refurbishment of the building. Developers must identify and remediate relevant defects, so that the fire safety risk associated with the building is reduced to a tolerable level.

Engaging with the Building Safety Regulator about a building covered by the Contract

Regulators may wish to engage with the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) where this would assist them in exercising their statutory functions, for example to obtain up-to-date information on any relevant BSR activity in relation to a building, including work undertaken by the Remediation Enforcement Unit, investigations, enforcement activity, Building Assessment Certificates, or building control matters. Regulators can contact the BSR Remediation Enforcement Unit at remediation@buildingsafety.gov.uk.

Using the Remediation Enforcement Support Fund for buildings covered by the Contract

The Remediation Enforcement Support Fund (RESF) is available to support local authorities and fire and rescue services with funding for legal advice on enforcement, including on buildings covered by the Contract. Guidance on the RESF is available on GOV.UK: Remediation Enforcement Support Fund​: application guidance.

If you apply to the RESF for a case involving a building covered by the Contract, the application will be considered alongside relevant information held by the team overseeing compliance with the Contract to ensure that decisions on applications are informed by the latest information about the building. We may contact you further to discuss this. If you would like to discuss a potential case before applying, contact: LocalRegulatorEngagement@communities.gov.uk.

Responding to emergency situations, such as potential decants, for buildings covered by the Contract

Where a potential decant relates to a building covered by the Contract, local regulators should contact MHCLG as soon as possible so that officials can raise the matter with the Participant Developer and discuss how the decant can be avoided or how residents can be supported where the decant is unavoidable. Early communication has often enabled action that avoided the need to decant the building and reduced distress and disruption for residents.

Imminent, statutory, or out of hours decants should be raised as soon as possible through: RedControl@communities.gov.uk. For decisions prior to statutory decants and non-statutory decants, local regulators should contact: LocalRegulatorEngagement@communities.gov.uk.

Where local regulators identify an emergency or serious building safety risk, they should consider whether the MHCLG Major Decants Protocol may be relevant to their circumstances. The Protocol provides a framework for managing large-scale resident decants arising from serious 11m+ building safety risks and sets out its own eligibility criteria and scope. Regulators should review the Major Decants Protocol to assess its applicability. Copies can be requested from: LocalRegulatorEngagement@communities.gov.uk.

The Protocol defines roles, reporting lines and coordination through Tactical Co‑ordination Groups (TCGs) and clear exit arrangements. Early notification by local regulators is encouraged, with TCGs convened for major decants. Short‑term evacuations of less than 24 hours would not normally trigger the Protocol unless impacts extend beyond that period. A decant refers specifically to the temporary relocation of residents to enable the mitigation of imminent risks to life relating to internal or external fire risks and structural defects, typically, though not always, following service of a Prohibition Notice.

Nothing within the Contract, associated processes or notification arrangements should delay emergency intervention by local regulators where immediate action is required to protect life.

For non‑emergency cases, regulators are encouraged to discuss proposed action with the Participant Developer and Responsible Person in the first instance, whilst keeping MHCLG informed via: LocalRegulatorEngagement@communities.gov.uk.

Responsible Entities

The Responsible Entity under the Contract and how it differs from the Responsible Person under fire safety legislation

The Responsible Entity and Responsible Person are distinct legal concepts that arise from different frameworks. In some cases, they may be the same organisation, but this will depend on the ownership and management arrangements for the building.

The Responsible Entity, defined in Annex 1 of the Contract, is the freeholder or superior leaseholder, including any building management company or managing agent acting on their behalf.

The Responsible Person is defined under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 and is the statutory fire safety duty holder responsible for fire risk management during occupation of the building.

MHCLG has published guidance to help Responsible Entities to understand how the Contract works: Guidance for Responsible Entities: Developer Remediation Contract.

Responsibility for updating the Responsible Entity on progress to assess or remediate a building

Participant Developers are obligated under the Contract to provide updates as often as reasonably necessary to the Responsible Entity about progress of remedial works. MHCLG expects the Responsible Entity to use this information to keep residents and leaseholders informed, but if a Responsible Entity is failing to pass on information, then MHCLG expects Participant Developers to find ways to send updates to residents and leaseholders directly.

Participant Developers are also obligated to establish processes to receive and promptly respond to communications from any of the leaseholders, residents, occupiers and other users of the buildings for which they are responsible (Clause 8). Many developers have established dedicated inboxes, and some have put in place resident portals to make it easier for residents and leaseholders to get information about their building.

If the Responsible Entity fails to pass on that information to residents and leaseholders, the Participant Developer must provide it directly to leaseholders, residents, occupiers or other users within 10 business days of a written request, at the Responsible Entity’s cost (Clause 8.4).

Audits of Participant Developers’ assessments

MHCLG regularly commissions independent audits of assessments provided by Participant Developers to make sure that they meet the Standards set out in the Contract (PAS 9980 for external defects and BS 9792: 2025 for internal defects), as well as checking that the conclusions of assessments are justified and that assessors are qualified, experienced, competent and independent (Clause 5.9 and Clause 11.2). Such audits do not replace independent regulatory assessment of fire safety risk.

Where an audit finds that assessment does not meet the requirements of the Contract, developers will be provided with the questionnaire completed by the auditor. MHCLG includes the auditor’s completed questionnaire in the audit outcome letter so that the developer can understand the reason(s) for the outcome of the audit and decide what action to take to address concerns raised by the auditor, where appropriate.

Developers should review this questionnaire and address any specific issues raised by the auditor, especially where the audit criteria have not been met. Developers will be given time to address these issues and typically re-submit the assessment. The assessments will then be audited again and the outcome shared with developers.

If an assessment obtained by a developer, or remediation works carried out by a developer, do not meet the required standard, the developer is contractually obligated to go back and put things right at its own expense.

Interim measures

Paying for interim measures

Under the Contract:

Participant Developers are not required to fund interim fire safety measures, including waking watches. Some developers have decided to fund interim measures in some buildings despite not being contractually obligated to do so

Participant Developers are obligated to fund moving residents out of a building to avoid an immediate or imminent threat to life or other personal injury, and where the works create or are reasonably expected to create circumstances with which residents cannot reasonably be expected to live. This includes any associated temporary accommodation costs (Clause 6)

Government has made grant funding available to support the installation of common fire alarm systems where interim measures are required. From 1 April 2026, this is provided through the £62.7 million Interim Measures Alarm Fund (IMAF), delivered by Homes England via the Cladding Safety Scheme platform. The fund is intended to provide a longer-term, sustainable alternative to waking watch arrangements and to protect leaseholders from the ongoing costs of interim measures while remediation is completed. Further information on the IMAF is available on GOV.UK: Interim Measures Alarm Fund (IMAF).

Annex A: Engagement with MHCLG on buildings covered by the Contract

This process map details how MHCLG can support information sharing and engagement in relation to buildings covered by the Contract. It should be read alongside the published Remediation enforcement: guidance for regulators. Decisions on regulatory activity and enforcement remain a matter solely for the relevant regulator(s).

Start.

Step 1: Building identified for inspection via a locally led, risk-based prioritisation programme.

Step 2: Identify lead regulator and gather relevant information, including through engagement with relevant regulators where appropriate.

Step 3: Is the building known or suspected to be covered by the Developer Remediation Contract?

- If yes, contact MHCLG at localregulatorengagement@communities.gov.uk to obtain developer contact details where relevant. Then continue to step 4.

- If no, end of process.

Step 4: Regulator to engage with developer and relevant parties to discuss remediation progress and relevant information.

Step 5: Has the developer responded and engaged with information requests?

- If no, regulator to notify MHCLG via localregulatorengagement@communities.gov.uk. The MHCLG division overseeing developer-led remediation will raise non-engagement with the developer. Return to step 4.

-If yes, continue to step 6.

Step 6: Regulator considers available information and determines any further action in accordance with its statutory functions.

Step 7: Where necessary, regulator may seek further information, specialist advice or legal support.

End of process.
